title: Earth Bulge Calculator: Midpoint Rise
description: Calculate the midpoint bulge of a straight line over distance with the Earth Bulge Calculator — the hump long links, canals and shots must clear. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, a perfectly straight line spanning 50 km has the Earth's surface bulging 49 metres up toward its midpoint — the hump every long radio link and canal survey must reckon with.
quick_answer: The Earth Bulge Calculator computes how far the Earth's surface rises toward the midpoint of a straight chord spanning a surface distance. Enter the span and read the bulge in metres or feet — the clearance a laser or radio path must allow for.

Extreme-range marksmen and surveyors both correct for the midpoint rise — over 5 km it is already about half a metre (0.49 m).
Water and light both refuse to follow the curve for free. The bulge is the first correction in any long, straight design.
The bulge is measurable with a theodolite and two boats — the number this page computes is the number those demonstrations keep finding.

A straight chord one mile long: the surface bulges toward its middle by 0.051 m — almost exactly 2 inches. Small at a mile, decisive at fifty kilometres (49 m). The bulge grows with the square of the span.
Twenty kilometres across: bulge 7.85 m at the midpoint — a two-storey house of planet standing in the middle of your 'flat' path, before any hill gets a vote.

popular_table.title: Midpoint bulge by span (spherical Earth)
popular_table.intro: Computed exactly as R − √(R² − (d/2)²) — the calculator's own formula.
popular_table.note: Bulge is measured at the midpoint, where it peaks. Off-centre, the rise follows the same circle geometry — the drop from a tangent is the Earth Curvature Calculator's framing of the identical fact.

faq: What is the difference between bulge and curvature drop?

Two views of one circle: drop is how far the surface falls away under a tangent line from one end; bulge is how far it rises toward a chord joining both ends. At the same distance the tangent drop is four times the midpoint bulge — geometry, not disagreement.
Exactly at the midpoint. A third of the way along, the rise is about 89% of the midpoint value — the circle's shoulders are broad.

For radio paths, yes: standard refraction bends rays slightly Earthward, modelled as a larger effective Earth (the 4/3 model on the Radio Line-of-Sight page), which shrinks the effective bulge. This calculator gives the pure geometric figure it is named for.
What about terrain between the endpoints?
The bulge is the planet's contribution only. Real clearance work adds terrain elevation, structures and vegetation on top — the Elevation Profile page supplies the terrain half.
Yes: the bulge is the sagitta of the Earth's arc, the surveyor's and astronomer's word for the same rise of the arc above its chord.
How long a span before it matters?
For centimetre-grade work, a few hundred metres. For eye-level judgements, around 5 km (half a metre). For radio links, always — it is in the standard path profile.
Does the bulge depend on direction?
On a sphere, no — the number follows the span alone. The real ellipsoid varies it by a fraction of a percent with latitude and azimuth, beneath most uses' concern.
